ui.basisH: What the story is based on
F00.title: What's real and what's made up
F00-1: Vivian and her five classmates are fictional; their stories are adapted from real reports and surveys.
F00-2: Every policy, slogan and amount has a source; numbers the game invented are marked.
F01.title: 2018: subsidized private preschools
F01-1: From August 2018, the government signed subsidy contracts with qualifying private preschools.
F01-2: Parents pay at most NT$4,500 a month; teachers must earn at least NT$29,000.
F02.title: 30% of teachers under NT$29,000
F02-1: Teachers' union survey: about 30% of preschool teachers earned under NT$29,000 a month; some operators counted bonuses toward it.
F02-2: Ministry of Education: the NT$29,000 excludes year-end and performance bonuses; pay records will be cross-checked.
F03.title: 2019: 1,063 subsidized preschools
F03-1: In 2019 there were 1,063 subsidized private preschools with over 110,000 places.
F03-2: Parents at a subsidized private preschool pay NT$4,500 a month.
F04.title: All 61 three-year-olds waitlisted
F04-1: In 2019, Taipei's public preschools dropped the 10 seats reserved for 3-year-olds.
F04-2: A Zhongshan District parent: after the 5- and 4-year-olds were drawn, all 61 three-year-olds were waitlisted.
F05.title: Public preschool lottery odds: 4% to 47%
F05-1: Teachers' union survey: public preschool lottery odds ran from 4% to 47%; more than half were under 30%.
F06.title: 2021: pandemic childcare leave
F06-1: When schools closed in May 2021, parents could take pandemic childcare leave; employers had to approve it and could not cut attendance bonuses.
F06-2: The Ministry of Labor did not require employers to pay for it.
F07.title: "The government will be parents' best teammate"
F07-1: President Tsai Ing-wen (May 7, 2021): the government will keep being parents' best teammate.
F07-2: The slogan at the same event: help people be "willing to marry, brave enough to have kids, happy to raise them."
F08.title: 92.5% of those who took the leave were women
F08-1: Awakening Foundation 2021 survey: women were 92.5% of workers who actually took pandemic childcare leave.
F08-2: Women worried the leave would hurt promotion, cost their jobs or cut their income.
F09.title: One tenant applies, the whole building pays
F09-1: After a college student applied for rent aid, the landlord raised rent by NT$1,000 for every unit in the building.
F09-2: Neighbors glared at him in the elevator, and he was bullied in the building.
F10.title: Target 500,000 homes, 278,000 applied
F10-1: The NT$30 billion rent subsidy aimed at 500,000 households; by the end of August 2022, about 278,000 had applied.
F10-2: A renter: her landlord said rent would rise at least NT$5,000 if she applied, so she gave up.
F11.title: Rent hikes: a survey and the ministry disagree
F11-1: Academia Sinica survey: about 24.3% of landlords surveyed raised rent.
F11-2: Ministry of the Interior, checking applications: rent stayed flat for about 93% and rose for about 6%.
F34.title: 2022: NT$30 billion rent subsidy
F34-1: In March 2022 the Cabinet launched a NT$30 billion rent subsidy, expanding it to 500,000 households.
F34-2: Extra for families with children: 1.4× for one child, 1.6× for two, 1.8× for three or more.
F12.title: 2022: child allowance of NT$5,000
F12-1: Child allowance: NT$3,500 a month from August 2021, NT$5,000 a month from August 2022.
F12-2: From August 2022: NT$6,000 a month for a second child, NT$7,000 for a third or later.
F13.title: After-hours care at public preschools
F13-1: From winter break 2024, after-hours care at public preschools has flat fees: NT$35 an hour on weekdays, NT$2,000 a month in school breaks.
F13-2: 2nd term of school year 2024–25: 95.35% of public preschools offered it; 540 extra care staff funded for 2025–26.
F14.title: Open till evening, no one to staff it
F14-1: Many counties keep public preschools open until 6 p.m., some until 7 p.m.
F14-2: Evening aides for children with special needs earn NT$183 an hour, and often no one takes the job.
F22.title: One teacher, a whole class, no time to drink
F22-1: Summer 2024: public preschools offered low-cost after-hours care for the first time.
F22-2: A rural public preschool teacher: one person watches the whole class, can't use the bathroom, doesn't dare drink water.
F15.title: 2025: public preschools open in school breaks
F15-1: From winter break 2024, after-hours care at public preschools during school breaks costs at most NT$2,000 a month.
F15-2: Before, parents paid for break-time care themselves, and it cost more than a private preschool.
F16.title: 2025: rent help for young couples and parents
F16-1: Starting 2026: rent aid rises 50% in the first 2 years of marriage, and another 50% for each child.
F16-2: Ministry of the Interior: if people dare to marry and have kids, the government will fully support them.
F17.title: 2026: parental leave by the day
F17-1: From January 1, 2026, unpaid parental leave can be taken by the day, up to 30 days, with 80% of pay covered by subsidies.
F17-2: At companies with fewer than 30 staff, the government pays the employer NT$1,000 for each day an employee takes.
F18.title: NT$800 a day for covering a colleague
F18-1: Cabinet population strategy: a first-ever NT$800-a-day allowance for workers who cover for a colleague.
F18-2: Parental leave becomes "childcare leave" for kids up to age 6, with 60 days that can be taken by the day.
F19.title: Shorter hours for parents, paid by the state
F19-1: Ministry of Labor plan: if a company lets parents of kids under 12 work shorter hours at full pay, the government covers the pay and funds a cover allowance.
F19-2: Labor Minister Hung Sun-han: aiming to start in 2027.
F20.title: Childcare leave bill in talks
F20-1: On October 8, 2026, party caucuses negotiated the gender equality in employment bill without agreement.
F20-2: The Ministry of Labor agreed to extend childcare leave to parents of kids up to age 8; the bill has not passed its final reading.
F21.title: Assisted reproduction law amendment
F21-1: The draft opens assisted reproduction to lesbian couples and single women.
F21-2: Committee review on July 16, 2026 did not finish; it will resume at a later date.

F23.title: 2018: what the story is based on
F23-1: Parents balk at Kevin's NT$10,000 fee: one mom estimated a public preschool costs about NT$2,000-plus a month, a private one at least NT$15,000.
F23-2: Kevin's preschool loses kids: the industry widely blames subsidized preschools for a "war for enrollment."
F23.game: "NT$10,000" and "fifteen fewer kids" are game numbers.
F24.title: 2019: what the story is based on (1)
F24-1: The boss says two hundred more this year: the first wave of subsidized private preschools numbered 200.
F25.title: 2019: what the story is based on (2)
F25-1: The boss's "2,247 classes in four years": Minister Lin Wan-i announced in 2018 that 2,247 public or nonprofit preschool classes would be added in 4 years.
F25-2: Parents asking each other about the lottery: in May and June, parent groups fill with "Did your kid get in?"
F25-3: Amy waitlisted: one mom said waitlists for 3-year-olds start in the hundreds.
F26.title: 2021: what the story is based on
F26-1: Amy can only take unpaid leave: pandemic childcare leave was a special unpaid leave.
F26-2: Jason gets extra shifts: when staff take parental leave, 70.6% of employers reassign the work within the same department.
F26-3: Coworkers without kids told to cover: a Dcard post, "So people without kids just have to cover?", struck a chord.
F27.title: 2022: what the story is based on (1)
F27-1: Jason's landlord adds NT$500: in real cases rent rose NT$1,000 for every unit, or at least NT$5,000 for anyone who applied.
F28.title: 2022: what the story is based on (2)
F28-1: Amy quits when her leave runs out: health ministry survey, 21.6% of women aged 15–64 left a job for 3+ months for marriage, childbirth or family care.
F28-2: How long until she can go back: women who quit to raise kids took about 5 years on average to return to work.
F28-3: HR asks about her two-year gap: 1111 survey, 98.6% say returning to work is hard.
F29.title: 2024: what the story is based on
F29-1: Jessica's 11-hour days: most preschool teachers add 2–3 hours of after-hours care, often working over 11 hours a day.
F29-2: Parents say after-hours care is the teachers' job: front-line teachers often stay until dark and take parents' complaints and late pickups.
F30.title: 2025: what the story is based on (1)
F30-1: The proposal in the boss's note: in 2023, Tainan's education chief Cheng Hsin-hui proposed capping break-time care at NT$2,000 a month.
F30-2: Jessica on summer duty: public preschools run break-time care to compete for enrollment; some stay open all eight weeks.
F30-3: "Earning money with no life left to spend it": the line comes from what front-line teachers told the preschool educators' union.
F31.title: 2025: what the story is based on (2)
F31-1: Wendy's mom says "people with a home dare to have kids": 1111 survey, 63.3% would be keener on marriage or kids if parents provided a home.
F31-2: Jason, single, comes last: an amended housing law reserves at least 20% of social housing for newlyweds (first 2 years) and families with children.
F32.title: 2026: what the story is based on
F32-1: Penny takes one day of parental leave: it can be taken by the day, up to 30 days; civil servants, teachers and military are covered too.
F32-2: Leave counted against her review: job-bank survey, 29.2% of married women were hinted their careers would suffer when pregnant; the most common problem was being hassled over short-notice leave.
F33.title: What Vivian's character is based on
F33-1: The low-birthrate office: a Ministry of Health and Welfare task force since 2017, with no real office or staff of its own.
F33-2: One-year contract, renewed by review: at the personnel agency, contract staff rated A or B are renewed; C means no renewal.
F33-3: The social media editor takes the blame: in 2023 the Education Ministry pulled a childcare ad, and its social media editor "Yating" apologized by name.
F33-4: Egg-retrieval days: egg freezing takes about 3–5 or more clinic visits; one cycle costs about NT$110,000–130,000.
